reviewBoundary: Three complete original senior paired readings: each three-question information text and four-question narrative/expository/argument text. Fictional notices and bounded workshop examples. Same-author all-option/text-evidence review only, no independent calibration.

units.title: An evening with the stars and an unexpected book
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A first evening of astronomy
materials.text:
The North Hill Learning Centre offers an introductory astronomy evening on Saturday,24 October, for students aged fifteen to eighteen. No knowledge of astronomy is required. Staff will begin indoors with a short explanation of the evening sky, then use the courtyard for observation if conditions allow.

Arrive at18:15 for registration. The indoor session starts at18:30, and the programme ends at21:00. Participants must remain with staff during the outdoor part. The centre supplies the equipment used in the session; personal telescopes are not needed and cannot be set up without agreement.

The fee is fourteen pounds. Book online by Wednesday, choosing one place for each participant. A request is confirmed only after the centre replies. Students under eighteen need parental or guardian consent; eighteen-year-olds complete their own form. Everyone provides an emergency contact.

Wear warm layers and suitable shoes. The courtyard may be colder than expected after the indoor talk. A hot drink is included, but participants should bring any personal water bottle they need. Food is not provided as a full evening meal.

Cloud does not automatically cancel the event. Staff may use prepared sky images and demonstrations indoors instead. The session introduces observation and interpretation, without guaranteeing a view of a particular object. If the centre itself cancels, confirmed participants receive a refund or another date. Contact staff before booking about access requirements.

questions.prompt: What should a beginner understand about the equipment?
options: Every participant must bring a telescope
Equipment is available only to experts
The centre supplies it
Personal telescopes can be set up anywhere
questions.explanation: Centre provides required equipment, personal setups need agreement. Other claims contradict access for beginners.

questions.prompt: When does registration begin for participants?
options: Wednesday midnight
questions.explanation: 18:15 arrival registration,18:30session,21end,Wednesdaybooking deadline.

questions.prompt: What may happen on a cloudy evening?
options: Every participant receives a meal instead
An indoor alternative is used
A particular star view is guaranteed
The event is always cancelled automatically
questions.explanation: Prepared images/demonstrations can replace observation. No automatic cancellation/view/meal promise.

materials.title: The book I had not asked for
materials.text:
For my birthday, my aunt gave me a collection of travel writing. I had asked for a novel by my favourite author, and the unfamiliar book felt like evidence that she had not listened. I thanked her politely and put it beneath two books I already knew I wanted to read.

A few weeks later, I needed something to read on a long journey. The novel was too large for my small bag, so I picked up my aunt's gift. I expected to read a few pages and fall asleep. Instead, I found an account of a town I had visited with my family.

The writer noticed things I remembered but had never put into words: the sound of shutters opening, the narrowness of a particular street, the way people waited outside a bakery. I did not agree with every judgement, but the familiar place made me curious about the next essay.

By the time I reached my destination, I had read half the book. I called my aunt to ask how she had chosen it. She said I often told detailed stories about places after trips. She had thought I might enjoy seeing how another person did something similar.

Her choice had not been random, although it had differed from my request. That did not mean every unexpected present was automatically perfect. It meant I had judged this one before discovering the attention behind it.

I finished the collection and lent it to a friend, then bought the novel I originally wanted with birthday money. There was room for both. My aunt's gift had not replaced my preference; it had added another possibility. Now, when I see its worn cover on the shelf, I remember the journey and the small surprise of discovering that someone had noticed a part of my interests I had not named myself.

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator initially disappointed?
options: The narrator has already read the collection
The book contains no writing
The aunt gives no present
The gift differs from the requested novel
questions.explanation: Expected favourite-author novel, received unfamiliar travel essays. Other reasons not stated.

questions.prompt: What first engages the narrator during the journey?
options: A letter written by the aunt on every page
A blank page for sleeping
An essay about a familiar town
A guaranteed prize inside the book
questions.explanation: Familiar town and observed details draw interest. Other objects/promises absent.

questions.prompt: How had the aunt chosen the book?
options: She noticed the narrator’s detailed stories about trips
She believed every reader likes identical books
She wanted the narrator to stop reading novels
She selected the cheapest cover without thought
questions.explanation: Aunt links existing travel storytelling interest. Other motives unsupported.

questions.prompt: What does the ending suggest?
options: Unexpected gifts must always replace chosen interests
Attention can be judged only by exact requests
The original novel becomes forbidden
A new possibility can accompany an existing preference
questions.explanation: Narrator enjoys both gift and wanted novel. Other absolute replacements contradict.

materials.title: Sketching in the local collection
materials.text:
The Eastgate Collection invites students aged sixteen and over to a half-day object-sketching workshop on Sunday,14 March,09:30–13:00. Participants observe selected objects from the public display and prepare a drawing with a short descriptive note. Artistic experience is not required.

Apply by the previous Monday with your preferred contact details. Places are limited to twelve. A place is confirmed by the organiser's reply, not by sending the application alone. The fee is ten pounds, including paper, pencils and a simple support board. Bring no paints, inks or personal sharp cutting tools into the gallery.

Meet at09:15 in the entrance hall. Bags larger than a small handbag must be left in the supervised storage area. Water can be kept there too; drinks are not taken into the object rooms. There is a break in the foyer halfway through the morning.

All observation takes place from the visitor side of barriers. The workshop does not provide handling access to original objects. Staff may supply a replica for one demonstration, clearly identified as such. A sketch should distinguish what you can see from details you have inferred.

The main rooms have step-free access, but contact the organiser in advance about other access needs. Participants keep their drawings. The collection may ask permission to reproduce selected work, but participation does not automatically transfer ownership or grant unlimited reuse rights.

questions.prompt: What is supplied for the workshop?
options: Unlimited handling of original objects
A large personal bag for every participant
Paper, pencils and a support board
Paint and ink for use beside originals
questions.explanation: Listed materials supplied. Paints barred/originals protected/bags storage not gift.

questions.prompt: What should a sketch distinguish?
options: Public access from permission to touch everything
Original objects from every possible replica without labels
The artist’s name from all evidence
Visible features from inferred ones
questions.explanation: Explicit observation-versus-inference rule. Other options distort or overstate.

questions.prompt: What does participation mean for reproduction rights?
options: All drawings must be published
Ownership automatically transfers to the collection
Permission must still be sought for selected work
Unlimited reuse is included in the fee
questions.explanation: Participants keep work; reproduction requested by permission. Other transfers/requirements denied.

materials.title: A sound without its picture
materials.text:
At a language workshop, the tutor played a short recording and asked us to describe it without naming what we thought caused it. I wrote, "A train arriving at a station." She asked me to try again. That was an interpretation, she said, not yet a description of the audible pattern.

I listened for a second time. There was a low continuous sound, several sharper clicks and a rise in volume followed by a gradual fading. Writing those features took more effort than supplying a familiar object. I had to separate what I heard from the story I had attached to it.

Other participants described similar features but suggested different sources. One imagined machinery in a workshop; another heard something moving across a bridge. The tutor did not use our disagreement to claim that all interpretations were equally supported. She asked which features each explanation accounted for and what additional information would help distinguish them.

The recording turned out to have been made inside a moving train. My first answer was related to the real source, but its arrival at a station was something I had invented. I had combined a reasonable identification with an unsupported event.

We then heard the clip with a photograph of the recording position. The picture helped, but it also directed attention. A participant noticed a rhythm he had overlooked when imagining a factory. The additional source did not simply add information; it changed how existing information was organised.

I left with a more precise vocabulary for sound and a better question about my own descriptions. What had I actually observed, and what had I supplied? The aim was not to remove interpretation from listening. It was to make the movement between observation and explanation clear enough to discuss.

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator asked to rewrite the first answer?
options: It refuses any possible source
It includes the exact recording position
It names an interpreted event rather than audible features
It is too detailed about clicks
questions.explanation: Train arriving supplies source/event before feature description. Other reasons contradict first response.

questions.prompt: What does the tutor do with differing interpretations?
options: Asks what each explains and what evidence could distinguish them
Declares every interpretation equally supported
Selects the loudest participant’s answer
Forbids further listening
questions.explanation: Evidence comparison explicit. Equality/no-listening/loudest rules not used.

questions.prompt: Which part of the first answer was unsupported?
options: The existence of audible clicks
Arrival at a station
Any connection with a train
A change in volume
questions.explanation: Inside moving train true; station arrival invented. Features audible, train related.

questions.prompt: What role does the photograph play?
options: It proves listening was unnecessary
It supplies a complete record of every journey
It adds context and redirects attention to the sound
It makes every earlier feature disappear
questions.explanation: Picture reorganises attention and reveals rhythm. Other absolute claims unsupported.

units.title: An essay call and a note below the page
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Essays on a place in translation
materials.text:
The Crossing Pages journal invites original essays about encountering a place through translated writing. Submissions may discuss one work or compare several, but should identify the particular translations used. The journal is interested in a reasoned reading experience, not a general ranking of national literatures.

Essays should be1,500–2,500 words, excluding references, and written in English. Include a brief biography of no more than80 words in a separate file. The main manuscript should omit the author's name for the first reading stage. This arrangement supports the review process; it does not promise that identity can never be inferred from content.

Submissions close on30 June. Acknowledgement of receipt is not acceptance. Contributors will normally receive an initial decision within eight weeks, although a request for revision may extend the process. The journal may decline an essay even after revision if it no longer fits the issue.

There is no submission fee. Authors retain copyright and grant publication rights under the agreement offered on acceptance. Quoted material must be referenced, and contributors are responsible for obtaining any permissions required for the proposed use. Finding a passage online does not settle that requirement.

Previously published essays are not considered. A short excerpt shared privately in a workshop is not treated as prior publication, but disclose any public posting when submitting. Questions about eligibility should be raised before the deadline. The editors will discuss uncertain cases rather than treat silence from an applicant as evidence that no issue exists.

questions.prompt: What must an essay identify?
options: Only the original title without translator information
A universal ranking of national literatures
The particular translations it uses
Every place the author has visited
questions.explanation: Call requires actual translations. Other conditions not requested or conflict with purpose.

questions.prompt: What does receipt acknowledgement mean?
options: The author has transferred all copyright
The submission has arrived, without acceptance guaranteed
Revision guarantees publication
The essay must be published within eight weeks
questions.explanation: Receipt explicitly not acceptance. Timing/revision/copyright other claims overstate.

questions.prompt: What should an author do about uncertain public posting?
options: Omit the required references
Assume silence proves no issue
Treat every private workshop as automatic publication
Disclose it and ask about eligibility
questions.explanation: Public posting disclosed; uncertain eligibility discussed. Other approaches contradict stated rules.

materials.title: The small note that changed the argument
materials.text:
A footnote can appear to offer merely supplementary detail. A reader may therefore feel free to pass over it, especially when the main text seems complete. Yet the location of information does not by itself determine its importance to an argument.

Consider a claim that a writer's position remained unchanged for decades. A note below the page may explain that the quotation comes from a revised edition rather than the first publication. That detail can affect the claim's historical basis. It is not decorative simply because smaller type and a lower position make it look secondary.

The reverse also matters. Not every footnote carries a hidden objection or essential correction. Some identify a source, define a term or acknowledge help. Reading responsibly does not mean treating every small note as a revelation that overturns the page. It means asking what work the note performs in relation to the claim above it.

Writers have responsibilities too. If a qualification changes the central meaning of a statement, placing it where readers are likely to overlook it may preserve apparent simplicity at the expense of fair communication. The fact that a caveat exists somewhere does not automatically make its presentation adequate.

A useful distinction is between keeping the main line readable and making a condition effectively invisible. These aims can be confused when a writer defends every omission from the paragraph by pointing to a note. The reader needs a reasonable opportunity to understand the scope of the claim, not merely a theoretical possibility of discovering its limit.

Footnotes can therefore support precision without becoming a separate territory where inconvenient information is stored. Their value depends on the relationship they create with the main text. A small note can strengthen an argument by exposing its basis; it can also reveal that the argument above requires a different formulation.

questions.prompt: What is the opening’s main point?
options: Small type always proves dishonesty
Main text never appears complete
Information’s position does not settle its argumentative importance
Every footnote is unimportant
questions.explanation: Position differs from evidentiary significance. Other universal claims rejected.

questions.prompt: Why is the revised-edition example used?
options: Footnotes cannot identify versions
Every revised edition repeats the first exactly
Revision dates are always decorative
A note can alter the basis of a historical claim
questions.explanation: Version detail may undermine unchanged-position claim. Other choices contradict example.

questions.prompt: What caution is made about readers?
options: They can infer importance only from font size
They should identify a note’s function without assuming every note overturns the argument
They should ignore all citations
They must regard every note as a secret correction
questions.explanation: Thirdparagraph distinguishes routine notes from consequential ones. Other extremes rejected.

questions.prompt: What responsibility does the writer have?
options: Hide all limitations to preserve readability
Move every source into the main paragraph without judgement
Assume a caveat anywhere always suffices
Make central qualifications reasonably available to readers
questions.explanation: Scope conditions need fair visibility, not mere theoretical discoverability. Other extremes not advocated.
